summary.text: Plankton are living things that drift in water or air and cannot push themselves against currents or wind.
Because the group is defined by how it lives and moves rather than by ancestry, it spans every major kingdom, from bacteria to jellyfish.
Plankton form the base of the marine food web, and the plant-like phytoplankton among them produce roughly half of Earth's oxygen.

facts.label: Size range
facts.value: From microscopic bacteria up to jellyfish

items.prompt: A jellyfish can pulse and swim slowly. Why is it still counted among the plankton?

options.label: It is closely related to drifting algae
It cannot generally overpower the currents
It spends its adult life on the sea floor
It makes its own food from sunlight

items.explain: Plankton are defined by being unable to beat the currents. Jellyfish swim, but not fast enough to generally overcome them.

items.prompt: Roughly how much of Earth's oxygen production comes from microscopic phytoplankton?

options.label: About 5 percent
About 20 percent
About half
Nearly all of it

items.explain: Phytoplankton photosynthesis accounts for roughly half of Earth's oxygen production.

items.prompt: The eastern Atlantic next to the dry Sahara is rich in phytoplankton. What best explains this?

options.label: Desert dust blown out to sea supplies iron
Rivers from the desert add fresh water
Desert heat warms the sea to ideal levels
Few fish live there to graze on them

items.explain: Iron reaches the ocean mainly as dust settling on the surface, and trade winds carry Saharan dust over the eastern Atlantic, feeding phytoplankton.

items.prompt: Large areas of the tropical open ocean get strong sunshine all year, yet produce relatively little plankton growth. Why?

options.label: The water there is too warm for photosynthesis
Strong waves keep plankton from settling
Too many whales eat the plankton there
Nutrients such as nitrate and phosphate are scarce

items.explain: Light is not enough on its own: these regions offer limited nutrients like nitrate, phosphate and silicate, so primary production stays relatively low.

items.prompt: A young sea urchin drifts in open water as a larva, then settles on the sea floor for the rest of its life. How does it fit the plankton?

options.label: It is plankton for its entire life
It is plankton for only part of its life
It never counts, since it ends on the floor
It counts only once it reaches the floor

items.explain: Meroplankton, such as sea urchin larvae, drift only for part of their lives before moving to a swimming or sea-floor existence.

items.prompt: Far below the depth where sunlight allows photosynthesis, zooplankton and bacteria still live. What do they mainly feed on?

options.label: Algae growing in the faint deep light
Sand and rock grains on the sea floor
Organic material sinking from the waters above
Nothing; they survive without eating

items.explain: At depths with no primary production, zooplankton and bacterioplankton consume organic material that sinks from more productive surface waters, known as marine snow.
